title: Guests with news
hookLine: angels visit Ibrahim, he hurries to feed them, and his wife laughs at the news of a son

cards: The doorbell rings, and nobody was expected. A quick inventory starts: anything in the fridge? Laundry on the couch?
Ibrahim, peace be upon him, gets that doorbell. Strangers arrive at his tent. They say peace, and he says peace back.
He doesn't know who they are. He doesn't ask what they want. The Qur'an says he slipped away to his household, quietly, and came back with a whole roasted calf.
Not a snack. A feast, for people he'd never met. Then something strange happens.

teach.b: The Qur'an tells this story twice, in Surah Hud and in Surah adh-Dhariyat, and each telling adds a detail. Surah Hud says he did not delay.
Adh-Dhariyat says he went to his family quietly, so the guests wouldn't feel like a burden, brought a fat calf and set it close to them. Then, gently: won't you eat?
That's hospitality in two verses: hurry, don't make a fuss, put the best you have within reach.
The Qur'an calls them the honored guests of Ibrahim, and the honor starts with the host.
They don't eat, and Ibrahim feels a flicker of fear. Commentators explain that in his world, a guest who refused your food might mean you harm. They say, don't be afraid.
They're messengers, angels, sent on to the people of Lut, with news for this house. His wife is standing nearby. The Qur'an doesn't name her; Muslim tradition knows her as Sarah.
She laughs. How can I bear a child, an old woman, with a husband this old? The angels answer: are you amazed at the command of Allah?
A son is coming, Ishaq, and after him a grandson, Ya'qub. Commentators don't agree why she laughed: the surprise, relief, the sheer impossibility. The text leaves it open.
Jews and Christians tell this visit too, at the oaks of Mamre in Genesis.

And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ made the host's side part of faith: a hadith in Bukhari says whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let them honor their guest. Ibrahim fed strangers before he knew they carried good news.

how: Welcoming guests with food and drink is a familiar part of Muslim home life, and teachers often cite the hadith about honoring the guest as the reason.

o: a merchant selling goods at market
a stranger who isn't to be trusted
a guest, someone welcomed and fed

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: laughed at the news of a son

s: Ibrahim knew the guests were angels when he fed them
he fed strangers. he only learned who they were when they wouldn't eat and told him not to be afraid.
the Qur'an tells this visit more than once
in Surah Hud and in Surah adh-Dhariyat, each adding details.
the Qur'an explains exactly why his wife laughed
it says she laughed. commentators have long disagreed about why.

games.q: you're Ibrahim. strangers arrive and greet you with peace. you don't know who they are. what do you do?
o: ask them politely what they want.
slip away and come back with a roasted calf.
offer water and wait to see if they stay.
games.why: he didn't delay: he went quietly to his household and brought a fat roasted calf, then set it near them. the feast came before any questions.

practice: Picture the people you'll cross paths with before tonight, a roommate, a coworker, a kid, and pick one.

Now picture what you could put within their reach: a coffee, half your lunch, a plate saved for later; Ibrahim brought a fat calf, and yours can be the best you have today, even if it's a granola bar.
If you pray, you can ask for an open hand.

wordCard.voice: Dayf, guest: the honored strangers Ibrahim fed before he knew they carried news of a son.

orig.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 51:24: "the honored guests of Ibrahim." dayf means guest.

carryVoice: Your line: hurry to the guest. In Ibrahim's tent, the food came before the questions. That's day thirty-eight.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6018; Sahih Muslim 47 (whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest)
Genesis 18:1–15 (the visit at Mamre, named as a neighbor)
